**The Weight of Silence**

The first time I understood the weight of silence, I was twelve years old, sitting on the edge of my bed with a half-eaten sandwich in my lap and the television humming in the background. My father had just left for work—again—without saying goodbye. Not that he ever did. But that morning, the silence in the house felt different. It wasn’t just the absence of his usual gruff *"See you later"* or the slam of the door. It was the way the air itself seemed to hold its breath, waiting for something that never came.

I picked up the sandwich and took a bite, but the bread tasted like dust. My mother was in the kitchen, scrubbing the same spot on the counter for the third time that week. She didn’t look up when I walked in. She never did anymore.

That was the day I learned that silence could be a kind of violence.

---

Years later, I found myself in a café in Paris, staring at a steaming cup of coffee I hadn’t touched. Across from me, a woman with sharp cheekbones and a cigarette dangling from her fingers watched me with an intensity that made my skin prickle. She didn’t speak. Neither did I. The space between us was thick, not with words, but with the unspoken: *Why are you here? What do you want?*

I wanted to ask her if she knew the story behind the scar on her wrist. I wanted to tell her about the night I’d stood in the rain for three hours because I’d missed the last bus and didn’t want to call my father for a ride. I wanted to confess that I’d spent the last six months writing letters I never sent. But the words stuck in my throat like swallowed glass.

She exhaled smoke, leaned forward, and said, *"You look like you’re waiting for something."*

I almost laughed. *"Aren’t we all?"*

She smiled, but it didn’t reach her eyes. Then she stood, dropped a few euros on the table, and walked out without another word.

---

Silence isn’t always the absence of sound. Sometimes it’s the absence of truth. The way my grandfather would nod along to my stories about college, his eyes glazing over as if he were listening, when really, he was already somewhere else—somewhere before my mother was born, before the war, before the silence that had settled into his bones like a second skeleton.

I asked him once why he never talked about it. He looked at me with those milky, faded eyes and said, *"Some things are better left unsaid."*

But I knew he was lying. Or maybe he was telling the truth in his own way. Maybe silence was his language, and I was too young to understand it.

---

There’s a kind of silence that comes with grief. The kind that fills a room when someone you love is gone, but no one says their name. The kind that makes you press your palms to your ears, as if you could muffle the echo of their laughter, their voice, the way they used to hum off-key in the shower.

I remember the first time I heard it. My best friend, Leo, had died in a car accident. His parents didn’t cry at the funeral. They didn’t scream, didn’t collapse. They just stood there, side by side, their faces smooth as stone. The silence was so loud it hurt.

Afterward, I went to Leo’s room. His bed was unmade, his clothes still strewn across the floor. I picked up a crumpled notebook from his desk, flipped through the pages. The last entry was dated three days before the accident:

*"I don’t know how to tell her. I don’t know how to tell anyone."*

I sat there for hours, reading those words over and over, until my eyes burned. I wanted to scream. I wanted to break something. But all I could do was sit in the silence, holding a notebook that would never be finished, a story that would never be told.

---

Silence can be a refuge. It can be a weapon. It can be the only thing left when the world has too many words.

I think about the times I’ve chosen silence. The way I’d bite my tongue during arguments with my ex, how I’d let my friends vent without offering my own pain, how I’d sit in therapy and stare at the floor instead of saying what I really meant. Silence as armor. Silence as escape.

But silence can also be a prison. The kind where you’re locked in with your own thoughts, with the things you’ve never said, the apologies you’ve never given, the love you’ve never let out.

---

Last night, I dreamed I was back in that café. The woman with the cigarette was there, but this time, she was sitting across from me, her hands wrapped around a cup of tea. She said, *"You’re still waiting."*

I woke up with my heart pounding. For what? For her? For my father? For Leo? For the version of myself who still believed in easy answers?

I don’t know.

But I know this: silence isn’t empty. It’s full of everything we’ve swallowed, everything we’ve choked on, everything we’ve been too afraid to let out.

Maybe that’s why we’re so afraid of it. Not because it’s quiet, but because it’s honest.

---

The world is full of noise. Alarms, sirens, chatter, the endless scroll of social media, the hum of engines, the clatter of forks on plates. We drown ourselves in it, thinking it will fill the gaps, thinking it will make us feel less alone.

But silence is the space between the notes. It’s the breath before the scream. It’s the pause that makes the next word matter.

And sometimes, the hardest thing to do is to sit in it.

---

I don’t know if I’ll ever learn to speak in the silences. Maybe I don’t have to. Maybe the point isn’t to fill them, but to listen—to the way the wind moves through the trees, to the way my own pulse sounds in my ears, to the way the world keeps turning even when we’re not looking.

Maybe silence is just another kind of language. One that doesn’t need words.

---

(Word count: 1,000)
